articles.title: Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey: the dullest, most pointless riposte possible to Christopher Nolan’s brilliant epic
articles.summary: It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t Think back. Do you remember when Elon Musk, in a weird online tantrum, and…
articles.content: It is hardly a shock that Grok AI’s interpretation of Homer is as meaningless as a laptop screensaver. The only surprise would be if Musk accepted defeat graciously. Which he won’t Think back. Do you remember when Elon Musk, in a weird online tantrum, and without having seen the film, condemned the supposed wokery in Christopher Nolan’s, The Odyssey, for getting Elliot Page to play Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o to play Helen of Troy? As the plaudits and the box-office receipts for Nolan’s Odyssey piled stratospherically up, Musk showed that being a good loser is not among his qualities. He petulantly exclaimed that he could do his own better and more authentic Odyssey on Grok AI. And now he has released the first online seven-minute “episode” to a world that has long since forgotten about this claim and didn’t care in the first place. In Musk’s version, as the tale begins Odysseus is – off screen – pretending to be mad to avoid fighting in the Trojan war. Grim-faced Palamedes and Agamemnon are shown testing this ruse by taking his baby boy Telemachus and placing him in the harm’s way of a plough in a field; Odysseus instantly rushes to save his child, showing that he isn’t mad, and agrees to fight. We see him join the armada, with Penelope and Telemachus (soon to grow to a little boy) left behind. This, effectively, is a prologue sequence that is not in Nolan. The expeditionary force arrives at Troy, and an intertitle tells us we have cut to a 10-years-later flashforward; the siege is about to escalate into the fake-horse attack. Continue reading...
articles.aiArticle:
When technology billionaire **Elon Musk** decided to pit his artificial intelligence against cinematic art, the resulting project emerged as little more than a hollow screensaver, according to a recent report by [Culture | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/27/elon-musk-ai-odyssey-movie-grok-christopher-nolan). The publication characterized the Grok AI-generated interpretation of Homer’s classic epic as an utterly pointless and tedious counter-response to acclaimed director **Christopher Nolan** and his masterworks. 

Rather than offering any genuine artistic insight, the output from the billionaire's chatbot serves up a sterile digital pastiche. The commentary notes that expecting a nuanced understanding of classical literature from an automated tool is bound to end in disappointment. Furthermore, the report suggests that accepting any creative shortfall with grace is entirely out of character for the tech entrepreneur, pointing to a history of defensive online outbursts whenever his ventures face creative or technical limitations.

## Historical Context and Broader Implications

This friction between high-profile tech figures and traditional media often intersects with broader regulatory and financial debates. As artificial intelligence models expand their footprint into creative domains, public scrutiny regarding their utility and cultural impact has intensified. For readers tracking the wider economic and political footprint of the tech sector, questions surrounding corporate power and government contracts remain pressing, as seen in our previous coverage regarding how to [Defund Elon Musk | Robert Reich](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/defund-elon-musk-robert-reich) and how the [US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-military-gives-elon-musk-s-spacex-access-to-sensitive-tracking-data). 

## Analysis: Why This Matters and What to Watch

*(Context: This section provides editorial analysis and does not represent reported facts.)*

The stakes here extend far beyond a simple internet spat over a movie comparison. As generative platforms increasingly attempt to replicate human storytelling, the line between automated noise and genuine artistic expression becomes a central battleground for the entertainment industry. Observers should watch for how Hollywood guilds respond to algorithmic encroachments on narrative traditions, as well as how tech companies pivot their marketing strategies when their AI-generated creative projects fall flat with critics and audiences alike.

articles.content: It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once proposed that rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money. They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. articles.title: Why won't MPs tax the rich? We asked them – and their answers gave us hope | Faiza Shaheen
articles.summary: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue In John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy…
articles.content: Even most Reform voters are in favour of a tax on the super-wealthy. Yet the first budget of the Burnham era looks set to dodge the issue In John Healey’s first budget this week, we will finally get a sense of the economic policies that will deliver Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism. Or will we? Capital gains tax equalised with income tax? Ruled out . A genuine wealth tax on those sitting on over £10m? Off the table . Even the briefed increase in the banking surcharge only takes us back to where it was until the Conservatives cut it in 2023. We can cross our fingers for trailed policies on supporting high streets, financial devolution and longer-term investment, but there is still more than a whiff of trickle-down economics in the air. Poll after poll shows that the British public overwhelmingly supports wealth taxes on the super-rich – including three in five Reform-leaning voters. We know that wealth inequality – with the richest 50 families in the UK possessing more wealth than half of the UK population – is weakening our economy , eroding our social fabric and undermining our democracy . Just last year, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, explicitly acknowledged that we have “ overtaxed labour and undertaxed wealth ”. So what on earth is going on? Faiza Shaheen is executive director of Tax Justice UK Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘If a person isn’t conscious, they’re not saying yes’: Cynthia Erivo on her searing new film about sexual assault
articles.summary: In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her…
articles.content: In Prima Facie, she plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual violence. Then she is raped by a colleague, and her world implodes. Erivo talks about the potential impact of the film – and how she is navigating her stratospheric success Cynthia Erivo is contemplating her favourite crisps, the ridged American brand Ruffles, as we sit talking in a quiet corner of a west London restaurant. Dressed all in black and sporting her signature elongated nails, she is known for her healthy lifestyle, but everyone, it seems, has their vices. “Ruffles are just perfect,” she says. “When you get a good batch, and the salt-to-potato ratio is perfect … it’s amazing.” Erivo has just touched down after singing in Phoenix, Arizona, the night before, and has been running me through the health routine that helps her maintain her frantic schedule. Before her concert, there was the Dior front row at Paris fashion week, and she has just been announced as a guest host on SNL UK. Erivo doesn’t drink alcohol (today she orders some peppermint tea); she’s vegan; she doesn’t eat airline food, only her own prepacked meals. She even has an infra-red sauna “to help me heal from the inside”. Earlier this year she ran the London Marathon before jumping on stage to perform Dracula, where she played all 23 parts; she had rehearsed her lines while going on gruelling marathon training runs. All that requires discipline – and snacks – to keep the show on the road. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘A dog would get treated better than a drag queen in Hollywood’: Alaska on prejudice and leading Oh, Mary!
articles.summary: The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy Alaska may be starring in the most subversive comedy in American theater today, but she carries herself with the poise of a 40s movie star. On a brisk…
articles.content: The RuPaul’s Drag Race alum on queer visibility, politics and starring in Cole Escola’s smash comedy Alaska may be starring in the most subversive comedy in American theater today, but she carries herself with the poise of a 40s movie star. On a brisk September afternoon, the actor, comedian and RuPaul’s Drag Race alumnus is in a small rehearsal room in New York’s midtown, sipping hot tea from a flask while perched on a hard-shell travel case. She sits bolt upright, as if she has spent her life balancing books on her head. It has been a madcap time for the actor as she prepares to play Mary Todd Lincoln in a new touring production of Cole Escola’s Tony award-winning comedy Oh, Mary! . She is amid a few weeks of rehearsals in the city before the show’s four-month sprint across the US. When I ask how she is handling the upheaval from her Los Angeles home, she smiles indulgently. “I mean, I would go to the planet Remulak for this show,” she says, referencing the home planet of the Coneheads . “I didn’t even think about it. I was just like, ‘Let’s make this happen.’” Continue reading...

articles.title: The One About Matthew Perry review – the star of one of TV’s biggest ever shows gets a loving tribute
articles.summary: This intimate, warm, thoughtful three-parter about the Friends actor speaks to his friends, family and ex-girlfriends – and their adoration for him is overwhelming “God, you can do whatever you want to me, just please make me famous.” So prayed Matthew Perry…
articles.content: This intimate, warm, thoughtful three-parter about the Friends actor speaks to his friends, family and ex-girlfriends – and their adoration for him is overwhelming “God, you can do whatever you want to me, just please make me famous.” So prayed Matthew Perry when he was a young unknown actor auditioning in LA, enjoying the partying and the friendships but struggling to find work. Many have offered up such a fervent wish, of course; few have had both sides of it fulfilled in such a spectacular way as the man who became part of one of the most successful sitcoms in television history and who died after relapsing into drug addiction in 2023 at the age of just 54. The three-part, three-hour documentary – titled, perhaps inevitably, The One About Matthew Perry – charts the whole of the actor’s rise and fall. It is an exhaustive but never (quite) exhausting film. Three hours is a long time, for sure, to tell what is in essence a sad but very simple tale, and some tiny trims could undoubtedly have been made, but it avoids tedium because of the quality of the interviews and the interviewees. The latter include his half-sister Mia and his best friends since his first days in LA, Roger Castillo and David Pressman. They all talk about the brother and the man with such love and such despair at the addictions he could not beat that it becomes at points not just a moving tribute to Perry but also to the thousands upon thousands of addicts and the people who love and despair of them, but whose stories don’t make international headlines. Continue reading...

articles.title: Michael Gambon: the authorised biography review – a brilliant actor, and a master deceiver
articles.summary: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unanswered Michael Gambon began his acting career with a preposterous bluff. Applying for a job at Dublin’s Gate theatre, the young toolmaker from the…
articles.content: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unanswered Michael Gambon began his acting career with a preposterous bluff. Applying for a job at Dublin’s Gate theatre, the young toolmaker from the south-east London suburbs embellished his CV with entirely fabricated theatrical experience. It was a gamble, but it worked. In 1962 he made his professional debut as the Second Gentleman in Othello. The following year he was hired by Laurence Olivier for the brand new National Theatre. Gambon carried on telling tall tales long after there was any need. Some were self-aggrandising: he had been a dancer with the Royal Ballet, worked as a nuclear physicist and auditioned for James Bond. To be fair, this last one was half-true – producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli had once called him in for a chat. Others were absurdities for the sake of it: he was thinking of buying a house in Hanoi, his mother had operated cranes in Dublin. Occasionally, the lies were intended to save his skin. Terrified of being sacked for turning up late yet again to rehearsal at the National, he claimed that his mother had died in the night. She went on to live for another 49 years. More often, he lied to make other people laugh, claiming that he had worked with the Russian director Dmitri Shagyerarsoff. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tiny zebra-striped bee in West a 'huge surprise'
articles.summary: A zebra-striped bee is seen in Somerset for the first time, offering hope in restored saltmarshes.
articles.content: A zebra-striped bee is seen in Somerset for the first time, offering hope in restored saltmarshes.
articles.aiArticle:
Conservationists in Somerset are celebrating an unexpected discovery after a striking zebra-striped bee was documented in the county for the very first time. According to BBC News, the sighting of this distinctive insect serves as an encouraging sign for local conservation initiatives aimed at reviving the region's coastal habitats. While researchers are still piecing together the implications of the finding, the presence of the insect has generated genuine excitement among wildlife experts tracking the recovery of the area.

## A Welcome Sign for Restored Saltmarshes

The appearance of the unusual insect was characterized as a massive surprise by specialists monitoring the ecosystem, as reported by BBC News. Wildlife advocates point out that the arrival of the bee in Somerset suggests that ongoing habitat restoration efforts in local saltmarshes are beginning to yield tangible ecological benefits. These coastal wetlands, which undergo frequent tidal inundation, require precise environmental conditions to support specialized wildlife, making the insect's presence a promising indicator of habitat health.

articles.title: Would you pay to have the ‘best baby’? Liberal eugenics and the troubling quest for human perfection
articles.summary: For decades the idea of eugenics has been taboo. Now it is returning in a new commercial guise For a very long time, I dreamed of being cured. I was born in 1981. I learned to walk early enough, but I stumbled and fell more easily than other children. My…
articles.content: For decades the idea of eugenics has been taboo. Now it is returning in a new commercial guise For a very long time, I dreamed of being cured. I was born in 1981. I learned to walk early enough, but I stumbled and fell more easily than other children. My parents began to worry that something was wrong, that my muscles were weaker than they should be. Eventually, at the age of three, I was diagnosed with a form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). In the 1980s, the precise mechanics were not yet understood, but the condition was known to be hereditary, probably linked to a recessive gene. It was also known to be progressive. As I aged, my muscles would not keep pace. At eight, I began to use a wheelchair for longer distances. By the time I was 18, I rarely walked outdoors any more. It is hard to be young and to know that you are growing weaker rather than stronger. I had all the same aspirations that my nondisabled friends did, but I lived in fear of the future in a way they did not. I spent a lot of time thinking about what my life would have been like if I didn’t have SMA. The images in my head were of something like a double: myself, only rid of this one deficit, imprecisely defined, but encoded somewhere in my body. Continue reading...

## Ethical Stakes and Societal Pressures

Historical eugenics movements relied heavily on coercion, sterilization, and state control, culminating in catastrophic human rights abuses. While contemporary practices emphasize parental choice and market access rather than authoritarian decrees, the underlying philosophy of grading human worth based on genetic markers alarms bioethicists. When reproductive choices become commercial transactions, lower-income families may be priced out of genetic enhancements, creating a biological divide that compounds existing economic inequalities.

The stakes involve not only fairness and access, but also society's foundational empathy toward disability and difference. As commercial entities market the promise of healthier or more capable children, individuals living with genetic conditions face renewed social stigma, subtly implying that their lives are mistakes that could and should have been prevented. 

## What Lies Ahead

Observer groups and regulatory bodies are expected to grapple with the commercial expansion of genetic screening technologies in the coming years. Policymakers face the delicate task of balancing reproductive autonomy with the prevention of discriminatory practices disguised as consumer choice. Meanwhile, public debate will likely intensify as more fertility startups offer polygenic embryo screening, forcing legal systems worldwide to define clear boundaries for the commercialization of human traits.

articles.content: 3Arena, Dublin Several unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon “We’d like to thank Ed Sheeran for organising this concert,” offers a member of Kneecap, one of several unannounced guests who have turned up for the first European date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour. It’s a characteristically two-fisted approach to the matter in hand from a band who have seldom shied away from controversy, but it has more than a grain of truth in it. The events of the last six weeks are quite something, and perhaps not what Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, had in mind when he led efforts to pressurise Sheeran to remove Macklemore from his summer US tour , after the rapper made a speech about Palestine on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Macklemore was duly removed from the tour, but the rapper saw his profile rise dramatically as a result – in fairness, he was hardly unknown, but his biggest hits are a decade old – while every other artist on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity . Sheeran’s tour limped on amid much opprobrium, while Macklemore was able to translate the publicity into a tour of his own, in noticeably bigger venues than he played on his last European tour, with proceeds donated to organisations assisting Palestinians. Dublin’s 13,000-capacity 3Arena is sold out, as is every other date on the tour. Continue reading...

The stakes for this new collaborative model are high, as independent verification is the cornerstone of credible scientific progress. articles.summary: Founder of an international organisation to encourage research into the rare genetic disorder Prader-Willi syndrome In 1984 Jean Phillips-Martinsson, a British woman living in Sweden, came across an article in the Lancet. It was about Prader-Willi syndrome…
articles.content: Founder of an international organisation to encourage research into the rare genetic disorder Prader-Willi syndrome In 1984 Jean Phillips-Martinsson, a British woman living in Sweden, came across an article in the Lancet. It was about Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS), a rare genetic condition named after Andrea Prader and Heinrich Willi, two of the three Swiss paediatricians who discovered it in 1956. It was a lightbulb moment for Phillips-Martinsson, who had been in limbo for 14 years, wanting to know why her son, Anders, born in 1970, was floppy and unable to suck as a baby, and later had behavioural problems and was constantly hungry (hyperphagia). It turned out these are all key signs of PWS. Continue reading...
articles.aiArticle:
An international advocacy network dedicated to studying a rare genetic condition has lost its founder, following the death of **Jean Phillips-Martinsson**. According to **Science | The Guardian**, her journey into medical advocacy began decades ago in **1984**, while she was a British expatriate residing in Sweden. Upon reading a medical article published in the Lancet concerning Prader-Willi syndrome, she discovered a distinct lack of cohesive global information regarding the disorder. 

Driven by this realization, **Phillips-Martinsson** placed an advertisement in a British newspaper to connect with other families facing the same diagnosis. This initial outreach led to a foundational meeting in **London** during **1985**, which brought together families from **Britain**, **Sweden**, and the **United States**. The report states that this gathering sparked the creation of international cooperation, eventually leading to the establishment of the **International Prader-Willi Syndrome Organisation** in **1990**, an entity she officially led as president until **1998**.

## Expanding Global Support and Research

Under her leadership, the organization grew substantially, holding its inaugural international conference in **Stockholm** during **1992** and gathering researchers from **17 countries**. According to **Science | The Guardian**, her efforts transformed isolated families into a globally coordinated movement capable of funding vital scientific inquiry. Her organizational model prioritized direct collaboration between parents and medical professionals, creating a unified front against a condition that was previously poorly understood.

As medical journalism continues to highlight individual contributions to public health—much like recent tributes to cultural figures such as the [Martina Arroyo obituary](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/martina-arroyo-obituary)—the loss of grassroots pioneers underscores how personal initiative can reshape institutional science. Prader-Willi syndrome is a complex genetic disorder that affects appetite, growth, and metabolism, often presenting severe lifelong challenges for patients and their caregivers. 

## The Broader Impact on Rare Disease Advocacy

> **Context:** The legacy of founders like **Phillips-Martinsson** illustrates why community-led initiatives remain vital in the medical sector. Rare diseases frequently struggle for funding and attention from major pharmaceutical bodies, making patient advocacy groups the primary engine for early-stage research and family support systems. Without such coordinated pressure, clinical understanding of rare genetic mutations often stalls for decades.

> **What to watch:** Observers will monitor whether international medical networks can maintain their grassroots momentum as founding generations step down, particularly as digital platforms change how rare disease communities organize and raise funds globally.

Sources: [Science | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/oct/26/jean-phillips-martinsson-obituary)

articles.title: The regime change we need for Thames Water | Letters
articles.summary: Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for…
articles.content: Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained ( Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October ) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question. Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed. Continue reading...

articles.summary: Nothing’s Ear 3A come in a variety of fun colors, including a yellow shade. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a…
articles.content: Nothing’s Ear 3A come in a variety of fun colors, including a yellow shade. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge If you want a decent pair of noise-canceling earbuds without spending a fortune, Nothing’s Ear 3A are worth considering. The wireless earbuds offer a lot of features for the price, and they’re an even better value now that all four colors are on sale at Amazon , Walmart , and Best Buy for $79 ($20 off), matching their all-time low price. Nothing Ear 3A earbuds Where to Buy: $99 $79 at Amazon $99 $79 at Walmart $99 $79 at Best Buy The Ear 3A deliver great performance for the price, with extensive EQ options that let you fine-tune the sound to your liking. My colleague John Higgins found the default sound a little too bass-heavy, but appreciated how easy it was to adjust — which is great, since that level of customization is unusual for earbuds at this price. While they won’t completely drown out chatter of your local coffee shop, the ANC does a good job of quieting low drones, including air conditioners and airplane cabin noise. We did encounter some bugs in testing, however, including abrupt changes in noise cancellation levels when using adaptive ANC, as well as occasional issues with voice calls in noisy environments. Still, they’re relatively minor drawbacks given what you get for the price. The Ear 3A also come in some fun colors — including a striking pink shade — and each pair includes extra-small ear tips for a more comfortable fit. articles.title: What the claw arcade game tells us about the cost of living crisis | Zoe Williams
articles.summary: No matter how you crunch the UK data, prices are rising while average wages stagnate. The system is rigged – and it’s time we kicked over the toy dispenser About a decade ago, the financial crash was almost a decade old. Unrelatedly, my kids were under 10, so…
articles.content: No matter how you crunch the UK data, prices are rising while average wages stagnate. The system is rigged – and it’s time we kicked over the toy dispenser About a decade ago, the financial crash was almost a decade old. Unrelatedly, my kids were under 10, so I was spending a lot more time in arcades. There’s a particular game involving a metal claw – it goes by the name of claw-game. You put in a pound, and try to manipulate the claw to grab a toy that is worth nothing like a pound. You would take that as the price of a bit of family fun, except the claw never grabbed a toy. The frustration for a six-year-old was immense, every lost pound making the probably flammable stuffed hamster more urgently desirable. But it was way worse for me, because I was clinging on to some residual 80s idea of arcade-honour. Surely, after pound #7, the machine would just give you a sodding toy? That would represent an astronomical return, lessen the possibility of an adult kicking the machine to death and assure a returning market of maybe 10% of the dumbest or most spineless parents. But no, nada. No toys, ever. Continue reading...

articles.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
articles.summary: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the…
articles.content: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...
